chunks: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)
about a jug in which a beetle was found, having died. He said: 'Throw it out and perform wudu from it; but if it was a scorpion, then discard the water and perform wudu from other water.'

And about a man who has two vessels with water, and filth fell into one of the two but he does not know which one it is, and he is unable to obtain any other water. He said: 'He should spill both out entirely and perform tayammum.'

key_terms.تَيَمُّم: tayammum — dry ablution using clean earth/dust, substituting for wudu when water is unavailable or impure
key_terms.جَرَّة: a large water jug or vessel, commonly used in classical Arabic households
key_terms.خُنْفَسَاء: a dung beetle or scarab; ruled not to cause ritual impurity of water
key_terms.عَقْرَب: scorpion; its death in water renders the water ritually impure per this ruling
key_terms.قَذَر: filth, dirt, or ritual impurity (najasah) that contaminates water

ai.seo_question: Does a beetle found dead in water make it impure for wudu according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) addresses two jurisprudential questions about water purity. The first concerns insects found dead in a water jug: a beetle does not render the water impure (the insect is removed and wudu proceeds normally), but a scorpion renders the water unfit for wudu. The second ruling addresses the situation of doubt where filth has fallen into one of two water vessels and the person cannot identify which one — in this case, both must be discarded and the person must resort to tayammum (dry ablution). These rulings reflect the classical Shia fiqh principle that certainty of purity is required for ritual acts, and that when purity cannot be established, the precautionary path (tayammum) is taken.
word_analysis: he should spill/discard both of them
